conclusion.justification: The report concludes that it remains unresolved whether benzodiazepines and related substances increase long-term dementia risk, noting that while associations exist in observational studies, stronger prospective studies point toward reverse causation or confounding rather than a established causal link. Because it treats the evidence as inconclusive and unresolved, it is best classified as hedged.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is closer to the current causal interpretation, but it is not a clean all-clear. Observational studies often find that benzodiazepine users are later diagnosed with dementia/Alzheimer’s more often; this demonstrates an *association*, not that the medicines cause dementia.

Evidence supporting a risk includes a large case-control study reporting Alzheimer’s disease was associated with prior benzodiazepine use (adjusted odds ratio 1.51; 95% CI 1.36–1.69), including after adjustment for anxiety, depression, and insomnia. A meta-analysis designed to address “protopathic bias” (early, as-yet-undetected dementia causing insomnia/anxiety and thus prompting prescriptions) nevertheless concluded the association was not *purely* explained by that bias.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25208536/  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-018-0535-3  

But the strongest counterevidence is an 8-year prospective cohort: dementia risk was slightly higher at *minimal* exposure, not at the highest exposure—a pattern incompatible with a straightforward dose-caused effect. Its authors concluded the findings did not support causality. A newer analysis likewise found patterns consistent with reverse causation/confounding and no significant association with long-term use.  
https://www.bmj.com/content/352/bmj.i90  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37312937/  

Thus, it remains unresolved whether benzodiazepines increase long-term dementia risk; a causal increase has **not** been established. Evidence for “Z-drugs” (e.g., zolpidem, zopiclone) is still thinner and similarly observational, so they cannot be assumed dementia-safe.

This uncertainty is not a reason for prolonged use: in older adults, benzodiazepines clearly increase short-term cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and dependence risk. Do not stop them abruptly; discuss gradual, clinician-guided tapering and non-drug insomnia/anxiety treatment with the prescriber.
